glossary.definition: An object that produces its own light.
An object seen by reflected light, not by its own emission.
A straight line showing direction of light travel.
A line perpendicular to a surface at the point of incidence.
Angle between incident ray and normal.
Angle between reflected ray and normal.
An image from which rays appear to come; rays do not actually meet there.
Spherical mirror with inward-curving reflecting surface.
Spherical mirror with outward-bulging reflecting surface.
Centre point of the mirror surface.
Centre of the sphere; lies on principal axis.
Point where parallel rays converge or appear to diverge from.
Distance from pole P to principal focus F.
Radius of the sphere; PC = R; often R = 2f.
Formed where light rays actually meet; can appear on a screen.
Bending of light when it passes between two media.
Ratio c/v; no unit; higher n means slower light.
Thicker at middle; converges light; f positive.
Thinner at middle; diverges light; f negative.
P = 1/f with f in metres; unit dioptre (D).
Ratio of image size to object size; sign shows orientation.

days.title: How We See and Represent Light

concepts.name: Luminous objects
concepts.simple_answer: A luminous object produces its own light. You see it because light travels from the object to your eyes.
concepts.why: Light must be emitted before anything can be seen in darkness.
concepts.example: The Sun, a burning candle, and a glowing bulb are luminous.
concepts.remember: Luminous means the object is the light source — not just bright-looking.
concepts.common_confusion: A white wall in daylight is not luminous; it reflects sunlight.
concepts.optional_detail: Luminous objects are primary sources of light in a scene.

concepts.name: Non-luminous objects
concepts.simple_answer: Non-luminous objects do not make their own light. We see them when light from another source reflects off them.
concepts.why: Most things around you — books, walls, the Moon — are seen by reflected light.
concepts.example: The Moon looks bright at night but shines by reflected sunlight.
concepts.remember: Non-luminous ≠ invisible. Reflection makes them visible.
concepts.common_confusion: The Moon is not a light source; it reflects the Sun's light.

concepts.name: Light source
concepts.simple_answer: A light source is where light begins in a situation. It may be natural (Sun) or artificial (torch).
concepts.why: Tracing from source → object → eye helps explain any seeing situation.
concepts.example: In a room, the bulb is usually the main light source.
concepts.remember: Always ask: where did the light start?

concepts.name: Reflected light
concepts.simple_answer: When light hits a surface and bounces back, that bounced light is reflected light.
concepts.why: Reflected light from non-luminous objects enters your eye so you can see them.
concepts.example: You see your face in a mirror because of reflected light.
concepts.remember: Reflection sends light back; it does not create new light.
concepts.common_confusion: Reflection is not the same as refraction (bending through a medium).

concepts.name: Light entering the eye
concepts.simple_answer: Vision happens when light from an object enters your eye and forms a signal for your brain.
concepts.why: No light entering the eye means no image — even if the object is there.
concepts.example: Light from a page reflects into your eyes when you read.
concepts.remember: See the path: source → object → eye.
concepts.common_confusion: The eye detects light; it does not send light out to see (unlike a common cartoon idea).

concepts.name: Seeing in darkness
concepts.simple_answer: In complete darkness there is no light to enter your eye, so objects cannot be seen — even if they are present.
concepts.why: Light is necessary for sight in the usual way we describe Class 10 optics.
concepts.example: In a closed dark room, a book on the table is invisible until you switch on a lamp.
concepts.remember: Darkness means insufficient light reaching the eye.
concepts.common_confusion: Some animals see with very little light, but you still need some light to enter the eye.

concepts.name: Straight-line propagation
concepts.simple_answer: In a uniform medium, light travels in straight lines. This is called rectilinear propagation.
concepts.why: Straight paths explain sharp shadows and why rays are drawn as straight lines.
concepts.example: Sunlight through a small window makes a sharp bright patch on the floor.
concepts.remember: Light rays are drawn straight until reflection or refraction changes direction.
concepts.common_confusion: Diffraction (bending around tiny openings) is a higher-class topic — not used in basic ray diagrams.
concepts.optional_detail: At very small scales light behaves as a wave; in Class 10 we use the ray model.

concepts.name: Ray of light
concepts.simple_answer: A ray is a straight line with an arrow showing the direction light travels. It is a useful model, not a thin physical beam.
concepts.why: Rays help us predict reflection and refraction without drawing every wave.
concepts.example: An arrow from a bulb to a book shows light travelling toward the book.
concepts.remember: One arrow = one direction of light travel.
concepts.common_confusion: A ray is a diagram tool; a real torch sends a wide beam of many rays.

concepts.name: Beam of light
concepts.simple_answer: A beam is a collection of many rays travelling together, often from a torch or sunlight through clouds.
concepts.why: Beams become easier to understand when you imagine many parallel rays side by side.
concepts.example: A laser pointer in fog shows a visible beam because dust scatters light.
concepts.remember: A beam = many rays; a ray diagram often shows one representative ray.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not look directly at the Sun or aim lasers at eyes — safety first.
concepts.optional_detail: Laser demos should be teacher-supervised only.

concepts.name: Source → object → eye
concepts.simple_answer: To explain seeing: light leaves a source, hits an object (often by reflection), then enters your eye.
concepts.why: This three-step model works for most everyday and NCERT situations.
concepts.example: Sun → Moon (reflect) → your eye: you see the Moon.
concepts.remember: Draw the full path before deciding where an image forms.
concepts.common_confusion: For a luminous object you may skip reflection off the object itself.

concepts.name: Reflecting surface
concepts.simple_answer: A reflecting surface sends light back instead of absorbing it. Polished mirrors reflect strongly; rough surfaces scatter light.
concepts.why: Only the reflecting side of a mirror matters for ray diagrams.
concepts.example: A calm pond reflects trees; a rough wall scatters light in many directions.
concepts.remember: Shiny and smooth surfaces give clearer reflections.
concepts.common_confusion: All surfaces reflect some light — even dull ones (otherwise we could not see them).

concepts.name: Incident ray
concepts.simple_answer: The incident ray is the incoming light ray that strikes a surface. The arrow points toward the surface.
concepts.why: Every reflection story starts with identifying the incident ray.
concepts.example: Light from a torch hitting a mirror is drawn as the incident ray.
concepts.remember: Incident = incoming; arrow points to the surface.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not confuse incident with reflected — direction of arrow matters.

concepts.name: Reflected ray
concepts.simple_answer: The reflected ray leaves the surface after reflection. Its arrow points away from the surface.
concepts.why: The reflected ray shows where light goes after bouncing.
concepts.example: In a mirror you see objects because reflected rays enter your eye.
concepts.remember: Reflected ray arrow points away from the mirror.
concepts.common_confusion: The reflected ray is not the same as the incident ray continued through the mirror.

concepts.name: Point of incidence
concepts.simple_answer: The point of incidence is the exact spot on the surface where the incident ray meets it.
concepts.why: Angles and the normal are always drawn at this point.
concepts.example: Where a laser dot hits a mirror is the point of incidence.
concepts.remember: Mark this point before drawing the normal.

concepts.name: The normal
concepts.simple_answer: The normal is an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.
concepts.why: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal, not from the surface.
concepts.example: At the spot where a ray hits a mirror, draw a dashed line at 90° to the mirror.
concepts.remember: Measure reflection angles from the normal, not from the mirror.
concepts.common_confusion: The normal and the reflecting surface are different lines.

concepts.name: Angle of incidence
concepts.simple_answer: The angle of incidence is measured between the incident ray and the normal at the point of incidence.
concepts.why: It tells how steeply light arrives compared to the normal.
concepts.example: A ray hitting head-on (along the normal) has zero angle of incidence.
concepts.remember: Use the arc between incident ray and normal — not the surface.
concepts.common_confusion: Measuring from the mirror surface gives the wrong angle (common error).

concepts.name: Angle of reflection
concepts.simple_answer: The angle of reflection is measured between the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence.
concepts.why: It describes how steeply light leaves after reflection.
concepts.example: If incidence is 30° from the normal, reflection is also 30° on the other side.
concepts.remember: Same side rule: both angles are measured from the normal on opposite sides of it.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not measure reflection angle from the mirror surface.

concepts.name: First law of reflection
concepts.simple_answer: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, when both are measured from the normal.
concepts.why: This law lets you predict the direction of the reflected ray.
concepts.example: A ray at 40° to the normal reflects at 40° on the other side of the normal.
concepts.remember: i = r (both measured from the normal).
concepts.common_confusion: Equal angles refer to incidence and reflection — not incident and refracted rays.

concepts.name: Second law of reflection
concepts.simple_answer: The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.
concepts.why: All three belong to one flat sheet — you draw them on one diagram plane.
concepts.example: When you tilt the mirror, the whole ray diagram plane tilts with it.
concepts.remember: Same plane means one 2D diagram is enough for plane mirrors.

concepts.name: Plane-mirror image properties
concepts.simple_answer: A plane mirror gives a virtual, erect image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
concepts.why: These properties explain why your mirror reflection looks life-sized and upright.
concepts.example: You appear to stand as far behind the mirror as you stand in front of it.
concepts.remember: Virtual + erect + same size + laterally inverted.
concepts.common_confusion: Virtual does not mean invisible — you see it, but light does not actually come from behind the mirror.

concepts.name: Spherical reflecting surface
concepts.simple_answer: A spherical mirror is part of a sphere's surface. Its curve affects how parallel rays converge or spread.
concepts.why: Curvature determines whether rays come together or spread apart.
concepts.example: A shiny inside of a spoon is roughly a concave spherical surface.
concepts.remember: Spherical = part of a sphere; not flat like a plane mirror.

concepts.name: Concave mirror
concepts.simple_answer: A concave mirror curves inward (reflecting surface faces the centre of the sphere). It tends to converge parallel rays.
concepts.why: Converging mirrors can form real images on a screen.
concepts.example: The inner surface of a spoon facing you acts like a concave mirror.
concepts.remember: Concave = cave-like = curves in.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not look at the Sun with a concave mirror — concentrated light can harm eyes.
concepts.optional_detail: NCERT paper-burning demo: teacher demonstration only, never unsupervised.

concepts.name: Convex mirror
concepts.simple_answer: A convex mirror curves outward. Parallel rays reflect as if coming from a point behind the mirror — they diverge.
concepts.why: Diverging mirrors give wide views — useful for safety mirrors.
concepts.example: The outer bulge of a spoon is like a convex mirror.
concepts.remember: Convex = bulges out toward the object.
concepts.common_confusion: Convex mirrors always give virtual, erect, diminished images for real objects.

concepts.name: Reflecting side
concepts.simple_answer: Only the shiny, inner or outer curved face reflects strongly. The back of a mirror is usually painted and non-reflecting.
concepts.why: Ray diagrams always use the reflecting side of the mirror arc.
concepts.example: In NCERT diagrams the shaded side is non-reflecting.
concepts.remember: Draw rays hitting the polished arc, not the back.

concepts.name: Pole (P)
concepts.simple_answer: The pole P is the centre point of the mirror's reflecting surface. It lies on the mirror itself.
concepts.why: P is often chosen as the origin in sign conventions.
concepts.example: The middle of a spherical mirror strip is the pole.
concepts.remember: P is on the mirror; C is not on the mirror.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not confuse P with F or C.

concepts.name: Centre of curvature (C)
concepts.simple_answer: C is the centre of the sphere of which the mirror forms a part. It lies on the principal axis, not on the mirror.
concepts.why: Distance PC equals the radius of curvature R.
concepts.example: For a concave mirror, C is in front of the reflecting surface.
concepts.remember: C is outside the mirror surface.
concepts.common_confusion: For convex mirrors, C is behind the mirror.

concepts.name: Radius of curvature (R)
concepts.simple_answer: R is the radius of the sphere. For the mirror, PC = R.
concepts.why: R links the mirror's size to its focusing strength.
concepts.example: If PC is 12 cm, then R = 12 cm.
concepts.remember: R = 2f for small-aperture spherical mirrors.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not use R and f as the same number without checking R = 2f.

concepts.name: Principal axis
concepts.simple_answer: The principal axis is the straight line through P and C, perpendicular to the mirror at P.
concepts.why: Most standard rays are drawn parallel to or through points on this axis.
concepts.example: Imagine a line through the middle of a spherical mirror strip.
concepts.remember: Principal axis passes through P and C.

concepts.name: Aperture
concepts.simple_answer: The aperture is the diameter of the reflecting surface. NCERT often uses small-aperture mirrors where R = 2f holds well.
concepts.why: Small aperture keeps the spherical mirror formula simple in Class 10.
concepts.example: The width MN of the mirror opening is the aperture in diagrams.
concepts.remember: Large mirrors break the small-angle approximation used in school formulas.

concepts.name: Mirror-type identification
concepts.simple_answer: Concave: reflecting surface faces inward. Convex: reflecting surface bulges outward. Compare which side is shiny.
concepts.why: Correct identification picks the right ray rules and image properties.
concepts.example: Shiny inside of spoon ≈ concave; shiny outside bulge ≈ convex.
concepts.remember: Ask: does the mirror surface hug the centre or push away from it?
concepts.common_confusion: Students often swap concave and convex — check the reflecting side.

concepts.name: Principal focus (F)
concepts.simple_answer: F is the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis converge (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex).
concepts.why: F is where parallel beams are focused or seem to spread from.
concepts.example: Sunlight parallel to the axis meets near F for a concave mirror.
concepts.remember: Label F on the principal axis between P and C for concave mirrors.
concepts.common_confusion: F is not the same as C — F is midway between P and C when R = 2f.

concepts.name: Focal length (f)
concepts.simple_answer: Focal length f is the distance from pole P to principal focus F along the principal axis.
concepts.why: f measures how strongly a mirror converges or diverges light.
concepts.example: If PF = 6 cm, then f = 6 cm (for that mirror).
concepts.remember: f is measured from P to F — not from C to F unless you know R = 2f.

concepts.name: Real focus
concepts.simple_answer: For a concave mirror, parallel rays actually meet at F after reflection. The focus is real — light converges there.
concepts.why: Real focus allows a hot spot on paper — teacher demo only, never at the Sun unsupervised.
concepts.example: Sharp bright spot on paper when sunlight is parallel to the axis.
concepts.remember: Real focus = rays actually cross.
concepts.common_confusion: Real focus does not mean the image is always erect.
concepts.optional_detail: Sun-concentration activities require adult supervision; use simulations when possible.

concepts.name: Virtual focus
concepts.simple_answer: For a convex mirror, reflected rays do not actually meet; they appear to come from F behind the mirror.
concepts.why: Virtual focus is found by extending reflected rays backward as dotted lines.
concepts.example: Convex rear-view mirrors seem to have a focus behind the glass.
concepts.remember: Virtual focus — extend rays backward to locate F.
concepts.common_confusion: Virtual focus is still a useful diagram point even though light does not cross there.

concepts.name: Converging mirror
concepts.simple_answer: A converging mirror brings parallel rays closer together. Concave mirrors are converging mirrors.
concepts.why: Converging mirrors can project real images onto screens.
concepts.example: Parallel rays from a distant object meet near F of a concave mirror.
concepts.remember: Concave = converging.

concepts.name: Diverging mirror
concepts.simple_answer: A diverging mirror spreads parallel rays apart. Convex mirrors are diverging mirrors.
concepts.why: Diverging mirrors give wider fields of view with smaller images.
concepts.example: Parallel rays reflect as if coming from F behind a convex mirror.
concepts.remember: Convex = diverging.

concepts.name: Parallel incident rays
concepts.simple_answer: Rays from a very distant object are nearly parallel to the principal axis when they reach the mirror.
concepts.why: Parallel rays are the standard starting ray in mirror diagrams.
concepts.example: Sunlight on a mirror is often drawn as parallel rays.
concepts.remember: Parallel to axis → reflects through F (concave) or appears from F (convex).

concepts.name: Reflected-ray behaviour
concepts.simple_answer: After reflection, concave rays converge toward F; convex rays spread so backward extensions meet at F behind the mirror.
concepts.why: Knowing the pattern lets you sketch images quickly.
concepts.example: Compare concave and convex diagrams side by side.
concepts.remember: Draw reflected arrows away from mirror; extend backward for convex.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not bend rays toward the wrong focus type.

concepts.name: Relationship R = 2f
concepts.simple_answer: For spherical mirrors of small aperture, radius of curvature R equals twice the focal length: R = 2f.
concepts.why: Links measurable R to the useful quantity f in problems.
concepts.example: If f = 5 cm, then R = 10 cm and PC = 10 cm.
concepts.remember: R = 2f → F lies midway between P and C.
concepts.common_confusion: Using f when you mean R (or vice versa) is a common numerical error.

concepts.name: Position of F between P and C
concepts.simple_answer: For a concave mirror, F lies on the principal axis between pole P and centre C — closer to P.
concepts.why: Order on axis: P — F — C for concave mirrors.
concepts.example: When marking a mirror setup, place F halfway between P and C if R = 2f.
concepts.remember: P–F–C order on the same side as the object for concave mirrors.
concepts.common_confusion: F is not at C unless f = R/2 still places F between them when R = 2f.

days.title: Concave Mirror Images: Object at a Distance

concepts.name: Object at infinity
concepts.simple_answer: When the object is very far away, its rays reaching the mirror are nearly parallel to the principal axis.
concepts.why: This is the starting case for many concave-mirror ray diagrams.
concepts.example: A distant tree or the Sun acts like an object at infinity.
concepts.remember: Parallel rays → image forms at focus F.
concepts.common_confusion: Infinity here means very far, not literally endless in problems.

concepts.name: Object beyond C
concepts.simple_answer: The object lies outside the centre of curvature — farther from the mirror than point C.
concepts.why: Image location and size change predictably as the object moves along the axis.
concepts.example: Place a candle beyond C on your marked principal axis.
concepts.remember: Object beyond C → real, inverted, diminished image between F and C.
concepts.common_confusion: Beyond C means object distance > R = 2f.

concepts.name: Object at C
concepts.simple_answer: The object is placed exactly at the centre of curvature C on the principal axis.
concepts.why: A special symmetric case: object and image distances are equal.
concepts.example: Object at C gives image also at C.
concepts.remember: Object at C → image at C, same size, inverted, real.
concepts.common_confusion: At C is not the same as at F.

concepts.name: Image position
concepts.simple_answer: Image position tells where rays actually meet (real) or appear to meet (virtual) after reflection.
concepts.why: You locate it on a ray diagram where reflected rays cross.
concepts.example: Mark where two reflected rays intersect — that is the image point.
concepts.remember: Real image: rays cross; virtual: extend rays backward.
concepts.common_confusion: Position is measured from pole P along the axis.

concepts.name: Image size
concepts.simple_answer: Image size compares how tall the image is relative to the object — enlarged, same, or diminished.
concepts.why: Size helps classify the image without doing calculations first.
concepts.example: A small distant image on a screen is diminished.
concepts.remember: Compare heights along a vertical line through the axis.
concepts.common_confusion: Size is not the same as magnification sign.

concepts.name: Image orientation
concepts.simple_answer: Orientation means whether the image is erect (same way up) or inverted (upside down).
concepts.why: Real images from concave mirrors are usually inverted.
concepts.example: A candle flame inverted on a screen is upside down.
concepts.remember: Inverted ≠ reversed left-right only — top becomes bottom.
concepts.common_confusion: Virtual images in concave mirrors can be erect.

concepts.name: Real image
concepts.simple_answer: A real image forms where reflected light rays actually meet. It can be projected onto a screen.
concepts.why: Real images carry light energy to a screen.
concepts.example: Activity 9.3: candle image on paper is a real image.
concepts.remember: Real image = rays actually intersect.
concepts.common_confusion: Real does not mean erect.

concepts.name: Screen formation
concepts.simple_answer: If a screen is placed at the image position, a sharp real image can be seen on the screen.
concepts.why: Screens catch light — only real images can be captured this way.
concepts.example: Move a paper screen until the candle image is sharpest.
concepts.remember: Only real images form on a screen.
concepts.common_confusion: Virtual images cannot be obtained on a screen.

concepts.name: Diminished image
concepts.simple_answer: A diminished image is smaller than the object in height.
concepts.why: Common when the object is far from a concave mirror.
concepts.example: Distant object beyond C → small inverted image.
concepts.remember: Diminished means shorter arrow, not farther away.
concepts.common_confusion: Diminished refers to height, not distance.

concepts.name: Same-sized image
concepts.simple_answer: When the object is at C, the concave mirror gives a real, inverted image the same size as the object.
concepts.why: The equal-distance case at C is worth remembering before moving the object closer.
concepts.example: Object height equals image height when object is at C.
concepts.remember: Same size at C only (for standard cases).
concepts.common_confusion: Same size does not mean erect.

days.title: Concave Mirror Images: Object Near the Focus

concepts.name: Object between C and F
concepts.simple_answer: The object sits between centre C and focus F — closer to the mirror than C but beyond F.
concepts.why: Image moves beyond C and grows as the object approaches F.
concepts.example: Candle between C and F → large real image beyond C.
concepts.remember: Between C and F → real, inverted, enlarged, beyond C.
concepts.common_confusion: This region is not the same as inside F.

concepts.name: Object at F
concepts.simple_answer: The object is placed exactly at the principal focus F of the concave mirror.
concepts.why: Reflected rays become parallel — image forms at infinity.
concepts.example: Object at F → parallel reflected rays, no sharp screen image.
concepts.remember: At F → image at infinity (theoretically).
concepts.common_confusion: At F is a limiting case, not a sharp image position.

concepts.name: Object between F and P
concepts.simple_answer: The object is between focus F and pole P — very close to the mirror.
concepts.why: Only here does a concave mirror give a virtual, erect, enlarged image.
concepts.example: Face close to a shaving mirror — enlarged erect view.
concepts.remember: Inside F → virtual, erect, enlarged, behind mirror.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not confuse with object beyond C.

concepts.name: Enlarged image
concepts.simple_answer: An enlarged image is taller than the object.
concepts.why: Magnification magnitude greater than 1 in size comparison.
concepts.example: Make-up mirror shows an enlarged face.
concepts.remember: Enlarged = bigger height, not necessarily real.
concepts.common_confusion: Enlarged virtual images are possible inside F.

concepts.name: Image beyond C
concepts.simple_answer: For an object between C and F, the real image forms beyond centre C.
concepts.why: Image distance increases as object nears F.
concepts.example: Object slides toward F → image slides farther past C.
concepts.remember: Object between C and F → image beyond C.

concepts.name: Image at infinity
concepts.simple_answer: When the object is at F, reflected rays are parallel and the image is said to be at infinity.
concepts.why: No single meeting point on the screen in the ideal case.
concepts.example: Sharp spot fails when object sits at F.
concepts.remember: Parallel reflected rays → image at infinity.
concepts.common_confusion: Infinity in diagrams means rays do not meet in finite space.

concepts.name: Image behind the mirror
concepts.simple_answer: For a virtual image, rays appear to come from a point behind the reflecting surface.
concepts.why: Draw dotted backward extensions to locate it.
concepts.example: Shaving mirror image seems behind the glass.
concepts.remember: Virtual image location is behind the mirror.
concepts.common_confusion: Behind the mirror does not mean inside the glass physically.

concepts.name: Virtual image
concepts.simple_answer: Light does not actually meet at a virtual image; the eye traces rays backward to see it.
concepts.why: You can see it but cannot capture it on a screen.
concepts.example: Mirror face view is a virtual image.
concepts.remember: Virtual = apparent meeting point only.
concepts.common_confusion: Virtual is visible — not invisible.

concepts.name: Erect image
concepts.simple_answer: An erect image has the same vertical orientation as the object.
concepts.why: Virtual images from concave mirrors (object inside F) are erect.
concepts.example: Your upright face in a close concave mirror.
concepts.remember: Erect = same way up as object.
concepts.common_confusion: Real images from concave mirrors are usually inverted.

concepts.name: Changing image properties
concepts.simple_answer: As the object moves from infinity toward P, image size, position, and nature change step by step.
concepts.why: Build the full table from observations, not memorisation alone.
concepts.example: Slide a candle along the axis and note each change.
concepts.remember: Track: position → size → nature (real/virtual) → orientation.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not jump to formulas before understanding the motion picture.

concepts.name: Convex-mirror focus
concepts.simple_answer: For a convex mirror, the focus F lies behind the mirror — a virtual focus.
concepts.why: Parallel rays diverge as if from F behind the mirror.
concepts.example: Rear-view mirror geometry uses virtual F.
concepts.remember: Convex F is always behind the reflecting surface.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not place F in front of a convex mirror.

concepts.name: Image behind a convex mirror
concepts.simple_answer: Convex mirrors always form images behind the mirror for real objects in front.
concepts.why: Consistent virtual image location simplifies safety mirrors.
concepts.example: Shop security mirror image appears inside the mirror.
concepts.remember: Convex → image behind mirror.

concepts.name: Virtual convex-mirror image
concepts.simple_answer: The convex-mirror image is always virtual — rays only appear to diverge from behind.
concepts.why: No screen image is possible for ordinary objects.
concepts.example: You cannot project a convex-mirror image on paper.
concepts.remember: Convex mirror → always virtual (for real objects).

concepts.name: Erect convex-mirror image
concepts.simple_answer: Convex mirrors always give erect images for objects in front of them.
concepts.why: Important for driving — up is still up.
concepts.example: Rear-view car mirror keeps orientation readable.
concepts.remember: Convex image is erect.
concepts.common_confusion: Erect here still means virtual.

concepts.name: Diminished convex-mirror image
concepts.simple_answer: Convex mirrors always produce diminished images — objects look smaller.
concepts.why: Smaller image allows a wider scene in the same mirror area.
concepts.example: Parking lot convex mirror shows many cars smaller.
concepts.remember: Convex → diminished.
concepts.common_confusion: Diminished helps wide field of view.

concepts.name: Wide field of view
concepts.simple_answer: A convex mirror curves outward so light from a large area reflects into your eye.
concepts.why: Used where seeing more area matters more than size.
concepts.example: Road junction mirror shows traffic from two directions.
concepts.remember: More area, smaller objects — trade-off by design.

concepts.name: Changing object position
concepts.simple_answer: For convex mirrors, image stays virtual, erect, and diminished — only position shifts slightly.
concepts.why: Less dramatic changes than concave mirrors.
concepts.example: Moving closer to a convex mirror — image still upright and small.
concepts.remember: Nature stays the same; position varies mildly.

concepts.name: Concave vs convex
concepts.simple_answer: Concave converges light; convex diverges. Image rules differ completely.
concepts.why: Pick mirror type before drawing any ray diagram.
concepts.example: Spoon inside vs outside surfaces.
concepts.remember: Concave: varied images; convex: always virtual, erect, diminished.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not apply concave ray rules to convex mirrors.

concepts.name: Plane vs convex
concepts.simple_answer: Plane mirrors give same-size virtual images; convex mirrors give diminished virtual images with wider view.
concepts.why: Choose mirror shape for the job: flat view vs wide view.
concepts.example: Bathroom flat mirror vs curved shop mirror.
concepts.remember: Plane: same size; convex: smaller but wider.

concepts.name: Rear-view mirror reasoning
concepts.simple_answer: Vehicles use convex rear-view mirrors because a wider, erect, diminished view improves safety.
concepts.why: You see more traffic even though cars look smaller.
concepts.example: Cars appear farther — compensate mentally when judging distance.
concepts.remember: Convex rear mirror: wide + erect + diminished.
concepts.common_confusion: Objects in mirror are closer than they appear — diminished effect.

concepts.name: Ray parallel to axis
concepts.simple_answer: A ray parallel to the principal axis reflects through F (concave) or appears from F (convex).
concepts.why: First standard ray for locating images.
concepts.example: Draw incoming ray horizontal to axis.
concepts.remember: Parallel in → through F out (concave).
concepts.common_confusion: Parallel means parallel to principal axis, not to mirror surface.

concepts.name: Ray through F
concepts.simple_answer: A ray through focus F reflects parallel to the principal axis.
concepts.why: Pairs with the parallel ray to locate images.
concepts.example: Ray from F hits mirror, leaves parallel to axis.
concepts.remember: Through F → reflects parallel to axis.
concepts.common_confusion: Reverse of the parallel-ray rule.

concepts.name: Ray through C
concepts.simple_answer: A ray through centre C reflects back along the same path (normal to surface at C).
concepts.why: Useful third ray when C is marked.
concepts.example: Ray aimed at C returns on itself.
concepts.remember: Through C → reflects back on same line.
concepts.common_confusion: C must lie on the path of the ray.

concepts.name: Ray at pole
concepts.simple_answer: A ray striking the pole P reflects symmetrically about the principal axis.
concepts.why: Optional fourth ray when image is near P.
concepts.example: Light hitting P reflects with equal angles to axis.
concepts.remember: At P, use reflection symmetry.
concepts.common_confusion: Not every diagram needs the pole ray.

concepts.name: Using two rays
concepts.simple_answer: Any two standard rays whose intersection locates the image are enough for a complete diagram.
concepts.why: More rays check your work; two are sufficient.
concepts.example: Parallel + through-F rays often meet at the image.
concepts.remember: Two correct rays → image point.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not draw random rays without rules.

concepts.name: Reflected-ray intersection
concepts.simple_answer: For a real image, draw reflected rays forward until they cross.
concepts.why: Crossing point is the top of the image.
concepts.example: Solid lines after mirror; meet at image.
concepts.remember: Real image = forward intersection.

concepts.name: Backward extensions
concepts.simple_answer: For virtual images, extend reflected rays backward (dotted) to find where they appear to meet.
concepts.why: Dotted lines mean virtual construction.
concepts.example: Convex mirror: extend rays behind mirror.
concepts.remember: Virtual image = backward extension meet.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not use dotted lines for real image formation.

concepts.name: Locating an image
concepts.simple_answer: Mark object tip, draw two standard rays, find intersection (or backward meet) — that is the image tip.
concepts.why: Repeat for base on axis to get full image arrow.
concepts.example: Image arrow perpendicular to axis from intersection.
concepts.remember: Tip-to-tip mapping: object tip → image tip.

concepts.name: Common ray-diagram errors
concepts.simple_answer: Typical mistakes: measuring angles from mirror, swapping F and C, wrong ray after parallel incidence.
concepts.why: Checklist prevents most exam losses.
concepts.example: If image looks wrong, redo rays from F and parallel rule.
concepts.remember: Verify: normal, F, C, arrow directions.
concepts.common_confusion: Reflected ray is not the incident ray continued.

concepts.name: Mirror applications
concepts.simple_answer: Concave: torches, dentists' mirrors, solar devices. Convex: rear-view and security mirrors.
concepts.why: Design follows image properties.
concepts.example: Headlight reflector is concave to parallelize bulb rays.
concepts.remember: Match mirror type to needed image.
concepts.common_confusion: Never aim concave mirrors at the Sun unsupervised.
concepts.optional_detail: Teacher demo or simulation only for concentration.

concepts.name: Pole as origin
concepts.simple_answer: In the mirror formula sign convention, pole P is taken as the origin (0) for distances.
concepts.why: All u, v, f are measured from P.
concepts.example: Distances start counting at the mirror surface.
concepts.remember: P = 0 on the axis.

concepts.name: Direction of incident light
concepts.simple_answer: Incident light is treated as travelling from left to right in standard NCERT diagrams.
concepts.why: Sets which side is positive for horizontal measurements.
concepts.example: Object usually placed to the left of mirror.
concepts.remember: Light goes left → right.

concepts.name: Positive horizontal
concepts.simple_answer: Distances measured along incident light (to the right of P in standard diagrams) are positive.
concepts.why: Object distance u is usually positive for real objects in front.
concepts.example: Real object in front → u positive.
concepts.remember: With the light: positive.

concepts.name: Negative horizontal
concepts.simple_answer: Distances measured against incident light (behind the mirror) are negative.
concepts.why: Virtual image distances are negative.
concepts.example: Image behind mirror → v negative.
concepts.remember: Against the light: negative.

concepts.name: Positive height
concepts.simple_answer: Heights measured upward from the principal axis are positive.
concepts.why: Erect object or image arrows above axis are positive.
concepts.example: Object above axis → positive height.
concepts.remember: Up from axis = +.

concepts.name: Negative height
concepts.simple_answer: Heights below the principal axis are negative — common for inverted images.
concepts.why: Magnification sign relates to orientation.
concepts.example: Inverted image arrow below axis → negative h′.
concepts.remember: Down from axis = −.

concepts.name: Sign of object distance u
concepts.simple_answer: For a real object in front of the mirror, u is taken positive in the NCERT convention.
concepts.why: Always check object placement before substituting.
concepts.example: Candle in front → u > 0.
concepts.remember: Real object in front → u positive.

concepts.name: Sign of image distance v
concepts.simple_answer: Real image in front: v positive. Virtual image behind mirror: v negative.
concepts.why: Sign of v tells real vs virtual quickly.
concepts.example: Screen image → v positive; mirror face image → v negative.
concepts.remember: Real v +, virtual v −.

concepts.name: Sign of concave-mirror focal length
concepts.simple_answer: For a concave mirror, focal length f is negative in the NCERT sign convention.
concepts.why: Same side as incident light for F but f carries a sign by convention.
concepts.example: Concave f = −|f| in formula work.
concepts.remember: Concave: f negative.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not drop the minus in 1/f.

concepts.name: Sign of convex-mirror focal length
concepts.simple_answer: For a convex mirror, f is positive — focus lies behind the mirror.
concepts.why: Opposite sign to concave for f.
concepts.example: Convex rear-view mirror: f positive.
concepts.remember: Convex: f positive.
concepts.common_confusion: Mixing concave and convex signs is a common error.

concepts.name: Object distance u
concepts.simple_answer: u is the distance of the object from pole P along the principal axis.
concepts.why: One of three key quantities in mirror numericals.
concepts.example: Object 20 cm in front → u = +20 cm.
concepts.remember: Measure u from P to object.
concepts.common_confusion: Use cm consistently until final step if needed.

concepts.name: Image distance v
concepts.simple_answer: v is the distance of the image from pole P along the principal axis.
concepts.why: Solve mirror formula for v after substituting u and f with signs.
concepts.example: Find v when u and f are known.
concepts.remember: v sign tells real vs virtual.

concepts.name: Focal length f
concepts.simple_answer: f links the mirror's curvature to focusing strength; insert with correct sign.
concepts.why: Concave f negative; convex f positive.
concepts.example: f = −15 cm for concave means |f| = 15 cm.
concepts.remember: Always include sign of f in 1/f.

concepts.name: Mirror formula
concepts.simple_answer: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f relates object distance, image distance, and focal length.
concepts.why: Use after sign convention is clear.
concepts.example: NCERT mirror numericals use this relation.
concepts.remember: Reciprocal form — not v = f + u.
concepts.common_confusion: This is not the lens formula.

concepts.name: Reciprocal quantities
concepts.simple_answer: The mirror formula uses reciprocals — compute 1/u, 1/v, 1/f separately with signs, then combine.
concepts.why: Avoid algebra mistakes by writing each term clearly.
concepts.example: 1/20 + 1/v = 1/(−10) style layout.
concepts.remember: Add reciprocals, not distances directly.

concepts.name: Substitution with signs
concepts.simple_answer: Substitute signed u, v, f before solving — signs are part of the physics.
concepts.why: Wrong sign → wrong nature of image.
concepts.example: Concave: f negative; real object: u positive.
concepts.remember: Signs first, numbers second.

concepts.name: Magnification m
concepts.simple_answer: Magnification compares image size to object size and can indicate orientation.
concepts.why: Connects heights and distances.
concepts.example: m = −2 means inverted and twice as tall.
concepts.remember: m negative → inverted; |m| > 1 → enlarged.

concepts.name: m = h′/h
concepts.simple_answer: Magnification equals image height divided by object height (with signs for orientation).
concepts.why: Use when heights are given directly.
concepts.remember: Negative m → inverted image.

concepts.name: m = −v/u
concepts.simple_answer: Magnification also equals minus image distance over object distance.
concepts.why: Useful when u and v are known from the mirror formula.
concepts.example: v = −30 cm, u = +15 cm → m = −(−30)/15 = +2 check signs carefully.
concepts.remember: m = −v/u with signed v and u.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not forget the minus in −v/u.

concepts.name: Interpreting m
concepts.simple_answer: After calculating m, state: inverted/erect, enlarged/diminished/same, using sign and |m|.
concepts.why: Numbers must become a physical sentence.
concepts.example: m = −0.5 → inverted, diminished to half.
concepts.remember: |m| size; sign orientation.

concepts.name: Transparent medium
concepts.simple_answer: Light can pass through a transparent medium — air, water, glass — with changed speed.
concepts.why: Refraction happens at boundaries between such media.
concepts.example: Glass window lets light through but bends it.
concepts.remember: Transparent ≠ no refraction.

concepts.name: Boundary between media
concepts.simple_answer: Refraction chiefly occurs when light crosses a boundary between two different media.
concepts.why: The surface is where speed changes.
concepts.example: Air–glass surface in a window pane.
concepts.remember: Boundary = interface between media.

concepts.name: Incident ray at boundary
concepts.simple_answer: The incident ray approaches the boundary; angle measured from the normal.
concepts.why: Same normal rules as reflection.
concepts.example: Ray from air into glass — incident in air.
concepts.remember: Incident ray in first medium.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not confuse with refracted ray.

concepts.name: Refracted ray
concepts.simple_answer: The refracted ray enters the second medium, bent at the boundary.
concepts.why: Direction of bend depends on speed change.
concepts.example: Pencil in water looks bent at surface.
concepts.remember: Refracted ray is in second medium.
concepts.common_confusion: Not the reflected ray.

concepts.name: Normal at boundary
concepts.simple_answer: Draw the normal perpendicular to the boundary at the point of refraction.
concepts.why: Angles of incidence and refraction are from this normal.
concepts.example: Same dashed normal idea as mirrors.
concepts.remember: Measure refraction angles from normal.
concepts.common_confusion: Normal is to the surface, not the mirror axis only.

concepts.name: Speed change
concepts.simple_answer: Light slows down or speeds up when entering a new medium — causing bending.
concepts.why: Root cause of refraction.
concepts.example: Light slower in glass than air → bends toward normal entering glass.
concepts.remember: Speed change → bending.
concepts.common_confusion: Higher optical density usually means lower speed.

concepts.name: Bending toward normal
concepts.simple_answer: When light enters a denser (slower) medium, it bends toward the normal.
concepts.why: Air to glass: ray moves closer to normal inside glass.
concepts.example: Straw in water appears broken at surface.
concepts.remember: Into denser medium → toward normal.
concepts.common_confusion: Toward normal ≠ along normal.

concepts.name: Bending away from normal
concepts.simple_answer: When light enters a rarer (faster) medium, it bends away from the normal.
concepts.why: Glass to air: ray moves farther from normal in air.
concepts.example: Ray leaving glass slab spreads from normal.
concepts.remember: Into rarer medium → away from normal.
concepts.common_confusion: Reverse of entering denser medium.

concepts.name: Optically rarer medium
concepts.simple_answer: The medium where light travels faster is optically rarer (e.g. air compared to glass).
concepts.why: Optical density is about light speed, not mass density alone.
concepts.example: Air is rarer than glass for light.
concepts.remember: Rarer = faster light.
concepts.common_confusion: Rare medium is not necessarily thin air only.

concepts.name: Optically denser medium
concepts.simple_answer: The medium where light travels slower is optically denser (e.g. glass compared to air).
concepts.why: Explains direction of bending at a boundary.
concepts.example: Glass is denser than air optically.
concepts.remember: Denser = slower light.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not equate to physical heaviness alone.

days.title: Glass Slab and Laws of Refraction

concepts.name: Air to glass
concepts.simple_answer: At an air–glass boundary, light slows and bends toward the normal on entering glass.
concepts.why: First step through a glass slab.
concepts.example: Ray from air strikes glass at an angle to normal.
concepts.remember: Air → glass: toward normal.

concepts.name: Glass to air
concepts.simple_answer: Leaving glass into air, light speeds up and bends away from the normal.
concepts.why: Second bend inside a slab.
concepts.example: Emerging ray in air bends away from normal.
concepts.remember: Glass → air: away from normal.

concepts.name: Rectangular glass slab
concepts.simple_answer: A rectangular glass slab has two parallel faces — two refractions occur.
concepts.why: Classic NCERT diagram.
concepts.example: Glass plate in optics kit.
concepts.remember: Two surfaces: enter and leave.

concepts.name: Emergent ray
concepts.simple_answer: The ray leaving the slab into the original medium is the emergent ray.
concepts.why: Compare direction to incident ray.
concepts.example: Light exits bottom of slab back into air.
concepts.remember: Emergent ray is after second refraction.

concepts.name: Parallel incident and emergent
concepts.simple_answer: For a parallel-sided slab, emergent ray is parallel to incident ray (laterally shifted).
concepts.why: Direction unchanged; position shifted.
concepts.example: Look through window — scene not rotated.
concepts.remember: Parallel in and out for rectangular slab.
concepts.common_confusion: Parallel does not mean same path line.

concepts.name: Lateral displacement
concepts.simple_answer: The emergent ray is shifted sideways relative to the incident path.
concepts.why: Offset depends on thickness and angle.
concepts.example: Thick glass shifts the view more.
concepts.remember: Shift sideways, same direction.

concepts.name: Angle of incidence
concepts.simple_answer: In refraction, angle of incidence i is between incident ray and normal at the boundary.
concepts.why: Same definition style as reflection.
concepts.example: Measure from normal in air before glass.
concepts.remember: i from normal, not from surface.

concepts.name: Angle of refraction
concepts.simple_answer: Angle of refraction r is between refracted ray and normal inside the second medium.
concepts.why: Pair with i for Snell's law at Class 10 level.
concepts.example: Smaller r than i entering denser medium.
concepts.remember: r in second medium, from normal.

concepts.name: First law of refraction
concepts.simple_answer: Incident ray, refracted ray, and normal lie in the same plane.
concepts.why: Same plane rule as reflection.
concepts.example: Draw all three in one 2D diagram.
concepts.remember: All three coplanar.

concepts.name: Snell's law (Class 10)
concepts.simple_answer: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r relates refractive indices and angles at a boundary.
concepts.why: Use with angles from normal.
concepts.example: Higher n side: smaller angle when entering denser medium.
concepts.remember: sin i / sin r = n₂/n₁.
concepts.common_confusion: Use degrees in calculator carefully.

concepts.name: Speed in vacuum c
concepts.simple_answer: c is the speed of light in vacuum, approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
concepts.why: Fastest possible speed for light.
concepts.example: Used as reference in n = c/v.

concepts.name: Speed in medium v
concepts.simple_answer: v is the speed of light in a material medium — always less than c.
concepts.why: Appears in refractive index definition.
concepts.example: Light slower in water than vacuum.
concepts.remember: v < c in any medium.

concepts.name: Absolute refractive index
concepts.simple_answer: Absolute refractive index compares light speed in vacuum to speed in the medium.
concepts.why: Material property for optics.
concepts.example: Glass has n around 1.5.
concepts.remember: n = c/v (absolute).

concepts.name: n = c/v
concepts.simple_answer: Refractive index n equals speed of light in vacuum divided by speed in the medium.
concepts.why: Main formula for Class 10 numericals.
concepts.example: If v = c/1.5, then n = 1.5.
concepts.remember: Bigger n → smaller v.
concepts.common_confusion: n has no unit.

concepts.name: Meaning of c
concepts.simple_answer: c is constant in vacuum — the upper limit for light speed used in the formula.
concepts.why: Numerator in n = c/v.
concepts.example: Same c for all materials in numerator.
concepts.remember: c is vacuum speed.

concepts.name: Meaning of v
concepts.simple_answer: v depends on the medium — water, glass, diamond each have different v.
concepts.why: Denominator sets n for each material.
concepts.example: Light slowest in diamond among common examples.
concepts.remember: Different media → different v.

concepts.name: Refractive index unitless
concepts.simple_answer: n is a ratio of speeds — it has no unit.
concepts.why: Do not write cm or m/s as unit of n.
concepts.example: n = 1.33 for water — just a number.
concepts.remember: Refractive index: no unit.

concepts.name: Higher n → lower speed
concepts.simple_answer: Larger refractive index means light travels slower in that medium.
concepts.why: Links table values to bending behaviour.
concepts.example: Diamond n high → light very slow.
concepts.remember: High n = optically dense = slower.
concepts.common_confusion: Higher n does not mean light travels faster.

concepts.name: Comparing media
concepts.simple_answer: Compare n values to see which medium is optically denser and how much light slows.
concepts.why: Used in refraction direction questions.
concepts.example: n_glass > n_air → glass denser.
concepts.remember: Compare n, then predict bending.

concepts.name: Physical vs optical density
concepts.simple_answer: A physically dense material is not always optically denser — optical density is about light speed.
concepts.why: Avoid everyday word confusion.
concepts.example: Kerosene may float on water yet have higher n.
concepts.remember: Optical density ≠ mass density.

concepts.name: Spherical lens
concepts.simple_answer: A lens is made of two refracting spherical surfaces — converging or diverging.
concepts.why: Base object for lens ray diagrams.
concepts.example: Magnifying glass is a convex lens.
concepts.remember: Two curved surfaces.

concepts.name: Convex lens
concepts.simple_answer: A convex (converging) lens is thicker at the middle than at the edges.
concepts.why: Parallel rays converge toward a real focus.
concepts.example: Magnifying glass converges sunlight — teacher demo only.
concepts.remember: Convex = thicker middle.
concepts.common_confusion: Never focus Sun on paper unsupervised.

concepts.name: Concave lens
concepts.simple_answer: A concave (diverging) lens is thinner at the middle than at the edges.
concepts.why: Parallel rays diverge as if from virtual focus.
concepts.example: Spectacle lens for some vision corrections.
concepts.remember: Concave = thinner middle.

concepts.name: Optical centre O
concepts.simple_answer: O is the central point of the lens through which rays pass without deviation.
concepts.why: Key point for one standard lens ray.
concepts.example: Ray through O continues straight.
concepts.remember: Through O → no bend.

concepts.name: Principal axis
concepts.simple_answer: Straight line through O perpendicular to the lens — symmetry line for diagrams.
concepts.why: Reference for foci and object placement.
concepts.example: Horizontal line through lens centre.
concepts.remember: Same role as mirror principal axis.

concepts.name: Two principal foci
concepts.simple_answer: A lens has two foci: F₁ on the incident side and F₂ on the other side.
concepts.why: Symmetric for thin lenses in air.
concepts.example: Mark F and 2F on both sides for convex lens.
concepts.remember: Two foci for thin lens in air.

concepts.name: Focal length
concepts.simple_answer: Focal length f is distance from optical centre O to principal focus F.
concepts.why: Use metres for power calculations.
concepts.example: f = 20 cm convex lens.
concepts.remember: Measure f from O to F.

concepts.name: Converging lens
concepts.simple_answer: Convex lens converges parallel rays — real focus on far side.
concepts.why: Used for real image formation.
concepts.example: Sunlight through convex lens — supervised demo only.
concepts.remember: Convex = converging.

concepts.name: Diverging lens
concepts.simple_answer: Concave lens spreads parallel rays — virtual focus on incident side.
concepts.why: Always virtual diminished images for real objects.
concepts.example: Concave lens in peepholes.
concepts.remember: Concave = diverging.

concepts.name: Thin-lens representation
concepts.simple_answer: Draw a convex or concave lens as a thin vertical line with outward/inward arrow symbols.
concepts.why: Standard NCERT shorthand.
concepts.example: Double-arrow line for convex; inward for concave.
concepts.remember: Thin lens: single vertical line symbol.

concepts.name: Ray parallel to lens axis
concepts.simple_answer: Ray parallel to axis refracts through F₂ (convex) or appears from F₁ (concave).
concepts.why: First standard lens ray.
concepts.example: Horizontal incoming ray bends through focus.
concepts.remember: Parallel → through F on far side (convex).

concepts.name: Ray through principal focus
concepts.simple_answer: Ray through F₁ (before lens) emerges parallel to axis after convex lens.
concepts.why: Pairs with parallel ray rule.
concepts.example: Through F in → parallel out.
concepts.remember: Reverse of parallel-ray rule.

concepts.name: Ray through optical centre
concepts.simple_answer: Ray through O continues undeviated.
concepts.why: Simplest third ray.
concepts.example: Straight line through middle of lens.
concepts.remember: O ray: no bend.

concepts.name: Convex-lens real images
concepts.simple_answer: Object beyond F → real, inverted image on opposite side (can screen).
concepts.why: Camera and projector principle simplified.
concepts.example: Object outside F forms screen image.
concepts.remember: Real when object beyond F.

concepts.name: Convex-lens virtual image
concepts.simple_answer: Object inside F → virtual, erect, enlarged image on same side as object.
concepts.why: Magnifying glass use.
concepts.example: Hold lens close to book — upright big view.
concepts.remember: Inside F → virtual erect enlarged.

concepts.name: Object at 2F
concepts.simple_answer: Object at 2F gives real, inverted, same-size image at 2F on other side.
concepts.why: Special symmetric case.
concepts.example: Mark 2F on both sides of convex lens.
concepts.remember: 2F object → 2F image, same size.

concepts.name: Object between F and 2F
concepts.simple_answer: Real, inverted, enlarged image beyond 2F.
concepts.why: Projector-like situation.
concepts.example: Slide projector object near F region.
concepts.remember: Between F and 2F → enlarged real image.

concepts.name: Object inside F
concepts.simple_answer: Virtual, erect, enlarged — magnifying glass mode.
concepts.why: Same as virtual image card — applied.
concepts.example: Reading fine print with magnifier.
concepts.remember: Inside F: magnifier.

concepts.name: Concave-lens image properties
concepts.simple_answer: Concave lens always gives virtual, erect, diminished image for a real object.
concepts.why: Only one nature — simpler than convex.
concepts.example: Peephole always small upright view.
concepts.remember: Concave: always virtual, erect, diminished.

concepts.name: Lens ray diagram
concepts.simple_answer: Use any two of: parallel→F, through F→parallel, through O straight to locate image.
concepts.why: Same strategy as mirrors.
concepts.example: Draw carefully to scale on axis.
concepts.remember: Two good rays enough.

concepts.name: Lens sign convention
concepts.simple_answer: Light travels left to right; distances against light are negative; f positive for convex, negative for concave (NCERT).
concepts.why: Mirror and lens signs differ — learn separately.
concepts.example: Convex converging lens: f positive.
concepts.remember: Lens signs ≠ mirror signs.

concepts.name: Convex-lens focal-length sign
concepts.simple_answer: Convex lens: f is positive in lens formula work.
concepts.why: Matches converging behaviour.
concepts.example: f = +20 cm for convex.
concepts.remember: Convex f positive.

concepts.name: Concave-lens focal-length sign
concepts.simple_answer: Concave lens: f is negative.
concepts.why: Opposite to convex.
concepts.example: f = −15 cm for concave.
concepts.remember: Concave f negative.

concepts.name: Lens formula
concepts.simple_answer: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f for thin lenses — note minus on 1/u term (different from mirror formula).
concepts.why: Most common mix-up with mirror formula.
concepts.example: Check NCERT lens numericals.
concepts.remember: Lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f.
concepts.common_confusion: Mirror uses plus between 1/v and 1/u.

concepts.name: Mirror vs lens formula
concepts.simple_answer: Mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. Learn both with correct signs.
concepts.why: Write which formula before substituting.
concepts.example: Label problem as mirror or lens first.
concepts.remember: Plus vs minus on 1/u term.

concepts.name: Lens magnification
concepts.simple_answer: m = h′/h = v/u for lenses (NCERT lens convention).
concepts.why: Sign of m gives orientation.
concepts.example: Compare to mirror m = −v/u.
concepts.remember: Lens: m = v/u.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not use −v/u for lens unless your text specifies mirror.

concepts.name: Interpreting lens m
concepts.simple_answer: State erect/inverted and size from sign and |m| after lens calculations.
concepts.why: Finish with words, not only numbers.
concepts.example: m = +2 erect enlarged (virtual case).
concepts.remember: Interpret |m| and sign separately.

concepts.name: Power of a lens
concepts.simple_answer: Power P measures converging/diverging strength: P = 1/f when f is in metres.
concepts.why: Used for spectacles and combinations.
concepts.example: f = 0.5 m → P = +2 D convex.
concepts.remember: P = 1/f (f in metres).
concepts.common_confusion: f must be in metres.

concepts.name: Dioptre
concepts.simple_answer: One dioptre (1 D) is the power of a lens with focal length 1 m.
concepts.why: Unit of lens power.
concepts.example: P = +1 D means f = 1 m convex.
concepts.remember: Unit: dioptre (D).

concepts.name: Focal length in metres
concepts.simple_answer: Convert cm to m before using P = 1/f — divide cm by 100.
concepts.why: Most common lens power mistake.
concepts.remember: Metres in power formula.
concepts.common_confusion: cm without conversion gives wrong P by 10⁴.
